id: I Ask My Grandmother If We Can Make Lahmajoun

Keywords: Sure, Tante, Lola

outputs.L1:
“Sure,” she says. “Why not?”

We buy the ground lamb from the market; we buy parsley, fresh tomatoes, and garlic. We cut, press, dice, and mix. We make the yeasty dough the night before, kneading it until our knuckles feel the hardness of riverbeds or rocks in the desert. We tell Tante Lola to come with her rolling pins; we tell Zaven and Maroush, Hagop and Arpiné, to bring their baking sheets.

We sprinkle flour across the kitchen table, and it is snowing on Ararat. We sprinkle the flour, and the memory of winter is in our eyes. We roll the dough into small circles—pale moons over every empty village. Kevork stands on a chair, singing, “O my Armenian girl, my spirit longs to be nearer.” Nevrig warms the oven, and a dry desert breeze skims over the rooftops toward the sea.

With our fingers, we spread the lahma on the ajoun, whispering into it the histories of those who have none. We bake them beneath the heat of the sun, the dough crisping until it is so thin and delicate that you would swear it was precious parchment. We take them out, roll them up in our hands, and eat, tasting once again everything that has already been written into the body.
outputs.L2:
“Of course,” she replies. “Why wouldn’t we?” We go to the market for minced lamb, parsley, ripe tomatoes, and garlic. We chop, crush, cube, and combine everything. The previous evening, we prepare the dough with yeast, working it until our hands encounter the firmness of desert stone and dry riverbeds. Tante Lola is summoned with her rolling pins, while Zaven, Maroush, Hagop, and Arpiné arrive carrying trays for baking.

Flour drifts across the kitchen table like snow falling on Ararat, bringing the image of winter back into our gaze. We flatten the dough into little round disks, each one resembling a faded moon suspended above an abandoned village. Standing on a chair, Kevork sings, “O my Armenian girl, my soul yearns to draw closer.” Nevrig heats the oven as an arid wind seems to sweep over the roofs and travel toward the sea.

With our fingertips, we spread the lahma over the ajoun, quietly pressing into it the stories of people whose histories have gone unrecorded. The oven bakes them as fiercely as sunlight. Their crusts become crisp, fragile, and so fine that they might be precious sheets of parchment. We remove them, curl them in our hands, and eat, rediscovering the taste of all that the body has long carried within it.
outputs.L3:
Preparing lahmajun is a shared, labor-intensive ritual that brings the entire family together. They gather the ingredients, mix them carefully, and knead the yeasty dough, each person contributing to the process. Relatives arrive carrying rolling pins and baking sheets, transforming an ordinary cooking task into a communal tradition shaped by cooperation, repetition, and affection.

As the family rolls, tops, and bakes the dough, images of Armenia enter the kitchen: Mount Ararat, deserted villages, and the sounds of Armenian songs. These memories intertwine with the physical work of preparing food, connecting the family’s present life to a homeland marked by displacement and loss. Spreading the mixture across each thin round of dough becomes more than a culinary step. It is a quiet way of preserving history and whispering the stories of people whose lives might otherwise be forgotten.

When the lahmajun is finally baked and shared, eating it becomes an act of remembrance. Through its familiar smell, texture, and taste, the family reconnects with experiences carried not only in stories but also in their bodies. The bread nourishes them while renewing a sense of cultural belonging, allowing memory to pass from one generation to the next.
outputs.L4:
The Armenian family gathers around the kitchen table to make lahmajun from scratch, repeating a ritual learned from parents and grandparents. Flour dusts the table as they knead the dough, roll it into thin circles, and prepare the topping of minced meat, tomatoes, peppers, onions, herbs, and spices. Everyone has a task. Some chop and mix, others shape the dough, spread the filling, or carry the rounds to the oven. Their movements are practical and familiar, but the work is more than preparation for a meal. Each gesture recalls another kitchen, another table, and the hands of relatives who once made the same food.

As they work, stories emerge. They remember villages their ancestors were forced to leave, recipes carried across borders, and family members who survived displacement by preserving whatever fragments of home they could. Measurements are given by instinct rather than written instruction: a handful of parsley, enough spice to awaken the meat, water added until the dough feels right. Such knowledge has passed from one generation to the next through observation and touch. Even when names, photographs, and official records have disappeared, the body remembers how to knead, season, fold, and share.

The communal labor turns the kitchen into a place where absence can be acknowledged. They speak of relatives they knew and of others whose lives can only be imagined. Some histories were silenced; others were deliberately erased. Yet the recipe remains, carrying traces of people who cannot tell their own stories. Making lahmajun becomes an act of resistance to that erasure. By preparing the food together, the family insists that their ancestors lived, cooked, gathered, and belonged somewhere. The meal preserves what history has tried to scatter.

When the lahmajun emerges from the oven, the dough is crisp at the edges and tender beneath the fragrant topping. The family squeezes lemon over the hot bread, adds herbs, and folds each round before eating. Taste collapses distance. The warmth, acidity, spice, and familiar texture connect them to places some remember directly and others know only through inherited stories. For a moment, homeland is not merely a lost territory or an idea described in the past tense. It is something immediate and physical, held in the hands and taken into the body.

Around the table, eating completes the act of remembrance that began with the mixing of dough. The family does not simply recall the past; they renew it and make it part of the present. Each shared piece of lahmajun affirms a continuity that displacement could not destroy. Food becomes an archive written not on paper but in flavor, movement, and communal practice. Through making and eating it, the family preserves identity, mourns what has been lost, and passes ancestral memory forward.

Whenever I visited her little house by the lake, she had a story to tell and something sweet to share. Tante Lola believed that even ordinary days could become special—with good food, kind words, and a little laughter.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about an Armenian family making lahmajoun together, blending recipe instructions with memories of homeland, diaspora, and inherited trauma.
counterfactuals.output:
**How to Make Lahmajoun**

Begin with flour, a white hill on the table. Press your fist into its center as if making a small country, a hollow where something might survive. Add yeast, warm water, salt, a thread of olive oil. Grandmother tests the water with her wrist. Not hot, she says. We have lost enough to fire.

Knead until the dough becomes tender and elastic, until it remembers how to return beneath your palm. Cover it with a clean towel and let it rise beside the radiator. In our family, even dough must learn exile: carried from bowl to bowl, from Aleppo to Beirut, from Yerevan to Marseille, from a village whose name is spoken only when the windows are closed.

While it rests, chop parsley until the cutting board turns green. Dice onion, garlic, tomatoes, and peppers. Mix with ground lamb, tomato paste, red pepper paste, black pepper, allspice, salt. Grandfather adds more Aleppo pepper, though he has not seen Aleppo in forty years. He shakes the jar over the bowl like a priest with incense.

Someone asks how much.

Enough, he says.

This is how the recipe has come to us: not in teaspoons, but in gestures. A palmful. A pinch. The red should look like sunset on stone. The meat should cling but not drown. The dough should be thin enough to see the shadow of your hand beneath it, but strong enough to carry what is placed upon it.

Divide the risen dough into small balls. Roll each one into a circle. Or something resembling a circle. Our maps have never stayed round. Borders tighten; borders tear. Still, Grandmother smooths each ragged edge with floury fingers and says, There. Beautiful.

Spread the mixture thinly, all the way to the rim. Do not heap it. Lahmajoun is not meant to bear too much.

But we heap everything: the photographs with their silvered corners; the brass coffee grinder; the key to a house no one living has entered; the silence of great-grandmother, who crossed a road without her sisters and thereafter could not bear the sound of marching feet. We inherit what was spoken and what was swallowed. Fear travels quietly through blood, changing its clothes at every border.

Bake in the hottest oven you have, on a stone if possible, until the edges blister and the meat darkens. The kitchen windows cloud. Children steal lemon wedges. An aunt slaps their hands without conviction. An uncle tells the same story about arriving at the airport with two suitcases and a violin. No one mentions that the violin had belonged to a boy who did not arrive.

When the lahmajoun emerges, squeeze lemon over it. Add parsley, sliced onion, perhaps a little sumac. Roll it while it is hot. Eat with both hands.

The first bite is bright with acid, smoke, and pepper. The second opens a door.

Beyond it: apricot trees lifting their small suns; laundry strung between balconies; church bells; sea wind; dust; a courtyard blue with evening. Beyond it, also, the road we do not describe. The hunger. The vanished names. The mothers who taught their children new languages but counted them in Armenian while they slept.

Make another. There are always more people than chairs.

Flour the table again. Let the youngest child roll the dough crooked. Let the eldest correct nothing. Tell the story of the mountain, whether or not the mountain can see us from here. Tell how yeast wakes when warmed. Tell how a people, too, may rise in a covered bowl, quietly doubling in the dark.

Serve the lahmajoun stacked beneath a towel so they remain soft. Pass them from hand to hand.

This is not the homeland, Grandmother says, looking around the crowded kitchen.

Then she tears one in half and gives the larger piece away.

For a moment, it is.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single-paragraph piece of poetic prose that begins with “Sure, she says, why not” and transforms the communal preparation of Armenian food into a meditation on history, family, and cultural survival.
counterfactuals.output: Sure, she says, why not, and rolls up her sleeves as if uncovering an inheritance, while the table fills with flour, parsley, cracked wheat, eggplant, and the bright red insistence of pepper; beside her, aunts pinch mantı into tiny boats, cousins press grape leaves around rice and herbs, and a grandmother measures everything by memory, her hands older than the recipes they carry. The kitchen clouds with steam and stories—villages renamed, photographs creased at the edges, journeys made with bread wrapped in cloth—until each dish becomes a small republic of what was nearly lost. They knead, chop, stuff, and season, arguing over salt, laughing in two languages, feeding the youngest from wooden spoons, and history, which arrived so often as hunger and silence, is answered with abundance: lavash swelling on the hot stone, dolma packed close as kin, choreg braided like the roads that scattered them. By evening, the table is crowded enough for the living and the dead, and when they sit shoulder to shoulder, passing plates from hand to hand, survival tastes not like endurance but apricot, smoke, garlic, mint—the old world made warm again, one mouthful at a time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe making lahmajun from scratch in a crowded family kitchen. Use a breathless, punctuation-light style, vivid imagery, Armenian names, and references to Mount Ararat, exile, and ancestral memory.
counterfactuals.output:
Flour spills across the table like first snow on Mount Ararat and Mariam is already elbow deep in the bowl calling for more warm water while Auntie Anahid wakes the yeast with sugar and Uncle Vartan insists the water must feel like a baby’s bath not hotter not colder

We pour and knead

flour yeast salt water a little olive oil

palms push forward fists fold back the dough softening beneath us while cousins squeeze past with trays and Grandmother Siranush guards the oven as if it contains the last fire carried out of the old village

The kitchen is too small for all of us and still everyone is here

Aram chopping parsley  
Lilit peeling onions  
Sarkis crushing garlic with the flat of his knife  
little Nare stealing red pepper strips and denying it with shining lips

The dough rests beneath a towel and swells quietly while the topping becomes a red fragrant storm

ground lamb and beef  
tomatoes squeezed of their water  
onion chopped nearly to a whisper  
garlic parsley green pepper  
tomato paste red pepper paste  
paprika Aleppo pepper black pepper salt  
a bright squeeze of lemon

Anahid mixes it by hand because spoons cannot remember what fingers know and she tells us spread it thin very thin this is lahmajun not meat pie and Siranush nods from her chair remembering another kitchen beyond the border beyond exile where her mother rolled dough on a low wooden board and Ararat stood on the horizon white shouldered and impossible to forget

We punch down the dough and divide it into small rounds

the rolling pins begin their clatter

Mariam rolls one crooked  
Vartan says it looks like Cyprus  
Mariam says eat your geography and rolls another

Each circle must be thin enough for light to almost pass through yet strong enough to carry the meat and we spread the mixture edge to edge with our fingertips no bare rim no heavy clumps just a scarlet skin of lamb tomato pepper and herbs

The oven is blazing as hot as it will go

trays slide in  
trays rush out  
someone opens the window  
someone shouts close it  
the glass clouds with steam and the room fills with roasted pepper caramelized onion hot bread and lamb fat hissing at the edges

The lahmajun emerge blistered and crisp but still supple and we stack them beneath clean towels so they soften in their own heat

Then comes lemon

then parsley

then sliced onion rubbed with salt and sumac

We fold each lahmajun in half and eat standing shoulder to shoulder because the table disappeared under flour bowls rolling pins and family long ago

Juice runs down Aram’s wrist  
Nare asks for another  
Siranush closes her eyes at the first bite

For one breath the crowded kitchen grows larger than the house larger than the city larger than exile

there is the lost courtyard  
the mulberry tree  
the stone oven  
the road not chosen  
the names carried from mouth to mouth

and beyond the window though we cannot see it Mount Ararat rises in ancestral memory while the next lahmajun comes burning from the oven and everyone reaches for it at once
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an evocative literary passage in which relatives gather to bake Armenian meat pies, and each step—kneading, rolling, topping, and eating—recalls lost villages, desert journeys, and stories carried in the body.
counterfactuals.output:
By noon the kitchen windows had clouded, though outside February pressed its white face to the glass. The aunts arrived carrying bowls under towels, onions in paper sacks, parsley beaded with cold. Uncle Sarkis brought the lamb, ground twice, and Grandmother brought nothing but her hands.

Those hands began the dough.

She poured flour onto the table in a pale hill and opened a hollow in its center. Into it went yeast, warm water, salt, a little oil. Her fingers circled slowly, drawing the walls inward.

“This is how the spring came down from the mountain,” she said, though no one had asked.

The younger ones knew the mountain only from stories: blue at dawn, purple in rain, standing above a village whose name had survived more faithfully than the village itself. Grandmother kneaded with the heels of her palms—push, fold, turn—until the dough grew smooth and living beneath her. Each push seemed to cross a distance. Each fold covered something that could not be left exposed.

Her mother, she told them, had kneaded dough in a courtyard where apricot branches leaned over the wall. Later, on the road south, there had been no flour, no courtyard, hardly any water. Still, her mother’s hands had made the motions against her skirt as she walked, remembering softness, remembering bread. The body rehearsed what the world had taken away.

They let the dough rise beneath a cloth.

While it breathed, the cousins chopped onions and peppers, tomatoes and parsley. The knife struck the board with the quick rhythm of hooves. Aunt Mariam mixed the vegetables into the lamb, staining her fingers red with pepper paste and paprika. She added cumin, black pepper, a pinch of something she would not name.

“From our village,” she said.

“But you were born in Beirut,” someone teased.

“And my mother in Aleppo. So what? The spice knew the way.”

When the cloth was lifted, the dough had doubled, a small astonishment. They tore it into balls and lined them on the table like pale stones. Uncle Sarkis rolled each one thin. Under the wooden pin, the rounds widened into maps—never perfect, their borders soft, their countries made and remade by pressure.

He spoke of a village beside a river, though he had learned it from his grandfather, who had learned it while trying not to forget. There had been a church bell, mulberry trees, ovens shared by neighbors. Every house had known the smell of everyone else’s supper. Then came the emptied rooms, the locked doors, the road unspooling toward the desert.

The rolling pin passed from hand to hand.

The children made crooked circles. The aunts corrected them gently. No one threw away a torn piece; it was pinched closed, dusted with flour, rolled again.

They spread the meat mixture to the edges with their fingertips. Not too thick, Grandmother warned. Let the dough carry it. The topping glistened with tomato and fat, green flecks of parsley bright as fields after rain. Tray after tray entered the oven.

Soon the kitchen filled with the scent of lamb, charred pepper, warm bread. It entered their hair and wool sweaters, their sleeves, the curtains. It seemed older than any photograph. It crossed borders without papers. It found the dead and seated them among the living.

They ate the pies hot, folding them around parsley and a squeeze of lemon. Juice ran down wrists. The first bite brought silence: crisp edge, tender center, sour brightness, heat.

Grandmother chewed slowly. Behind her closed eyes were the vanished houses, the desert where names had been swallowed by wind, the mothers who hid songs under their tongues and carried recipes without measures, without ink, without certainty of arrival. What survived had not survived whole. It had come folded, scorched, altered by every oven along the way.

Still, there it was in their mouths.

The children reached for another. The adults began contradicting one another about whose mother used garlic, whose village used more pepper, whether the dough should be thinner. Their voices rose warmly, familiarly, each argument another proof of inheritance.

Outside, snow erased the street. Inside, flour marked every hand.

Grandmother looked around the crowded table and smiled. Then she took a piece of dough left beneath the cloth and placed it before the youngest child.

“Push,” she said, guiding the small palms with her own. “Fold. Turn. Again.”

And beneath their hands, the past—stubborn, wounded, fragrant—began once more to rise.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose poem about food as cultural memory, centered on Armenian relatives preparing lahma ajoun with lamb, parsley, tomatoes, garlic, and homemade dough. Make the tone intimate, communal, and haunting.
counterfactuals.output:
On Sundays, the table disappeared beneath the work of remembering. My aunts bent over bowls of lamb, parsley, tomatoes, and garlic, their hands shining with oil, their voices crossing the kitchen like threads pulled through old cloth. Someone rolled the homemade dough thin as a letter from the dead. Someone salted the meat without measuring. No one needed a recipe; each gesture had survived by entering the body.

We called it lahma ajoun, shaping the syllables with mouths already hungry. The children carried the rounds to the oven, solemn as candle-bearers, while the elders corrected us gently—more filling at the edges, press with your fingertips, do not tear what must hold. Heat lifted the scent of garlic and lamb into every room. The windows clouded. For a moment, the house became larger than itself, opening onto orchards we had never seen, courtyards erased from maps, stones warm beneath the feet of relatives whose names we carried but whose faces had faded.

When the bread came out blistered and fragrant, we folded it around parsley and ate shoulder to shoulder. Tomato ran down our wrists like a bright wound. Everyone spoke at once; everyone listened for those who were missing. The dead sat nearest the oven, invisible and famished, warmed by what we remembered to make.

By evening, only flour remained on the table, pale as ash. My grandmother swept it into her palm and would not throw it away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
